paragraphs.text: John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople, on the Resurrection of Christ. From Luke the Evangelist: And behold, two of them were traveling along the road that day to a village sixty stadia away from Jerusalem, called Emmaus. Oh, how, when fear and terror seize a mortal, his whole being is immediately thrown into turmoil! Oh, how the high priests’ threats shook the apostolic trumpets [?]! Oh, how the rulers’ audacity drove away the company of apostles! Oh, how the rulers’ ferocity disturbed the disciples’ minds! For mortals seized the Maker of all, and just as wild beasts seize a lamb, so the killers of God seized Christ and brought him into the high priest’s courtyard. Then the chief apostle was struck down by denial. John fled and went away. Thomas was held captive by unbelief.

And behold, two of them were walking. In fear they said: Let us flee the beasts; in fear let us escape the beasts. In fear let us escape the deadly prisons. As they said these things to one another: Let us flee the high priests’ audacity. Let us escape the rulers’ murderous hands. For even if they hand us over to death, we will not bear their insults. And even if they do not shed our blood, they will pierce us with words. Let us flee the high priests’ rage. Let us escape the scribes’ threats. Let us run away, so that we are not overtaken as we go. Let us turn aside from this road, so that we do not encounter savage tongues. For they killed the shepherd and tore the sheep apart. They killed the helmsman; they will drown those who were with him in the depths. They walked along thinking these things. Indeed, in truth, they were like those sown beside the road. For a wind of fear blew upon them and shook their whole being like leaves. And behold, two of them were walking that day. You did not even wait until the third day, of which he had told them, but at the very hour when they nailed Life to the tree, when they laid the Immortal One among the dead, when the Lord’s murderers sealed the tomb, on that very day the two were walking away. They did not wait for the time when Christ was to overthrow Hades. When the one who had been buried was about to release the captives held for many days. When the one numbered among the dead was about to break the seals of the tomb. When the one lying in the tomb as in a womb was about to roll the stone away from the tomb. When the one numbered among the dead was about to put the guard to death.

When, appearing weak, he shattered the barriers of death. When, appearing naked, he was about to take the ungodly one captive. But at that moment the two did not wait to see this. Instead, they fled at that moment and spoke to one another about everything that had happened. For they were reflecting within themselves on his great deeds. How did the one who performed such signs endure being seized by wicked hands? How did the one who performed so many miracles choose to be arrested—the one who changed the nature of water into wine? He fed an immeasurable multitude with a few loaves. In the wilderness he drove out a multitude of demons with a word. He uttered a word and drove away diseases. He sent forth a word, and afflictions departed. With mud he restored the pupils of the eyes. He called to the dead as though they were asleep. With a word he called the lame to run. He healed the paralyzed man and made him carry his own bed. He walked on the surface of the sea as though on dry ground. He calmed a windstorm with a word. Grasping the hem of his garment stole healing from him. He made tax collectors into apostles. He guided a weeping prostitute into the realm of heaven. These were the things the two said and discussed with one another. These deeds truly display the power of God. These deeds are far beyond mortal nature. These deeds truly belong to an immortal being, not a mortal one. Yet again, the two formed a less exalted opinion among themselves: He wore flesh [?] and lived just like a human being. He ate bread and grew thirsty. He walked on his feet and grew tired. He rested and served

the needs of his nature. He reclined at table with tax collectors and lived among prostitutes. He endured insults, and when he was belittled, he remained silent. He was overcome with fear during his suffering and said, Now my soul is troubled. He was arrested and could not flee. He was bound and could not escape. He was condemned and could not prevail. He was nailed to the cross and could not come down. He was given vinegar to drink. And he did not give bitterness to drink in return. He was pierced with a spear, and his blood flowed out with water. And again, these things are human and mortal. They truly belong to our nature, and are not immortal. The two were reflecting on all these things that had happened. And while they were talking, and questioning each other about what had happened and what was to come, the Savior himself drew near and walked with them. The helmsman of souls appeared to resolve their dispute. The Sun of righteousness came and spread over them a ray of divinity and knowledge of God. The one they were seeking appeared. And Jesus himself walked with them, but their eyes were kept from recognizing him. He changed their eyes, however, so that they would not recognize him then, for he was keeping himself hidden, so that he might reveal himself to them at the breaking of the bread. “What are these words that you are exchanging with each other as you walk, and why are you sad? For even if you wish to lie, your faces reveal your sorrow. Tell me, what are these words that you are exchanging with each other? Tell me too about the conversation you are having. I too will take part in the words you are exchanging. What, then, are these words that

you are exchanging with each other as you walk, and why are you sad? Your faces cry out about your grief.” One of them, whose name was Cleopas, answered and said to him, “Are you the only person living in Jerusalem who does not know what has happened? Granted that you have not seen it, have you not heard it? Even if you were not there to see it with your eyes, did you not hear it with your ears? Even if you were not there when these things happened, have you not heard what happened? Have you neither seen nor heard what happened? Are you the only person living in Jerusalem who has not learned what happened in it? Have you not even heard the outcry? Has creation not taught you what happened? Have the elements not taught you by undergoing change? The sun stripped itself of light and clothed itself in darkness. The moon’s beauty suddenly grew dark. The curtain of the temple was torn into strips. Day changed its clothing into night. The rocks broke into pieces. The power of Hades was bound. And have you not learned what happened? Are you so gripped by ignorance, O man, that you do not understand this? Are you a stranger to these places? Have you only now come into this city, as we suppose? You are from another nation if you have not learned this. Creation was changed, and could you not see it?” Are you the only person living in Jerusalem who does not know what has happened there in these days? He said, “What marvelous event has happened in the world, something foreign to mortal nature, and appeared in creation? What? What I suffered for your sake, what I [?] for your sake, and endured to save you? But what is it? Tell me, you two. If anything marvelous has been done by people,

show it to me. If anything new has appeared in creation, what is it?” Cleopas said, “I did not lie, sir: you are indeed a stranger to these parts. If you know nothing at all, tell me. But if it is only the suffering that you do not know about, I will tell you about it.” But he kept saying, “What?” “Listen, sir.” At once came the name and place of origin: “The things concerning Jesus of Nazareth. Jesus by name, from Nazareth by origin. He was a prophet, fulfilling what was written and teaching about things to come. He was a prophet, of whom Zechariah said, ‘Behold the man whose name is the East.’ With a single word he drove away afflictions; with a single utterance he banished illnesses. He was a prophet, mighty in deed and word. He rebuked the sea, and it grew calm: mighty in deed and word. He stripped away leprosy as though it were clothing: mighty in deeds. He commanded the winds, and they gave way: mighty in word. He touched those burning with fire, and they cooled down: mighty in deeds. He spoke to Hades, and it brought out those who were decaying: mighty in word. Taking five loaves, he fed a multitude: mighty in deeds. A word demolished words, and he sent crowds of demons into pigs: mighty in word. He touched a withered hand, and immediately sent it to work: mighty in deed. He cursed a fig tree, and it withered: mighty in word. He anointed eyes with mud and restored sight: mighty in deeds. The council of the chief priests he cut down with a word: mighty in word and deed. He drained away the fluid of dropsy: mighty in word and deed. The chief priests came to test him, and with a single word he silenced them. When they wanted to put him

to the test, they became his disciples. When they wanted to learn something from him, they asked him for signs. But a word demolished words, and he cut down their council: mighty in word and deed. before God and all the people. The chief priests and rulers handed him over to be condemned to death. And they crucified him. They placed the uncondemned before the judgment seat, as one to be condemned before Pilate. They brought him before Caiaphas like a criminal. They bound his hands, though he had worked so many miracles. They nailed down his feet, which had cut through the waves of the sea. They hung Life on a tree. They [?] “You shall not kill.” They pierced him with a spear. They rejected “You shall not bear false witness,” and they gave false testimony. They handed him over to be condemned to death. And Pilate, after having him beaten, handed him over. And the people cried out, “Away with him! Away with him! Crucify him!” But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel. Oh, how Luke recalled all of Cleopas’s fear! He did not say [?], “We hope,” but “We had hoped that he would redeem Israel.” “We thought,” he said, “that he would save the nations. We rejoiced that he would save the people.” As I think, Cleopas had lost hope concerning Christ. When Cleopas had spoken [?], Jesus said to them, “O foolish ones, slow of heart to believe everything the prophets spoke! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things?” Well does the one called a stranger teach those who teach. Well does the one wishing to learn silence those who teach. “O foolish ones, slow of heart, because you did not believe

the prophets, that Christ had to suffer in this way and so enter into his glory.” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he explained to them the things concerning himself in all the Scriptures, that Christ had to suffer in this way. Beginning with Moses, the friend of God, the foremost of the prophets, who was the first to write the words, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He taught them that Moses had said, “You will see your life hanging before you.” And the one who was hung said, “I am the life and the resurrection.” Jeremiah said, “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will scatter.” And the one who was struck said, “I am the good shepherd, even though you too fled, overcome by fear.” David said, “The one who eats my bread has greatly increased his treachery against me.” And he himself said at supper, “One of you will betray me.” Before his suffering he said, “Now my soul is troubled.” And during his suffering he said, Now the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. David said, “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.” And after drinking, he said, “It is finished.” Likewise also concerning the Passion. David beforehand [?]: “They laid me in the lowest pit, in dark places and in the shadow of death.” Asaph, concerning the resurrection: “Arise, O God, judge the earth.” Jacob: “He slept like a lion and arose like a lion cub.” Jonah, by spending three days in the whale, foreshadowed his resurrection on the third day. David, concerning the ascension, truly, truly proclaimed with a trumpet: “God has ascended with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet.” To him be glory, and through him to God the Father, in the Holy Spirit,
as in the beginning, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
